title: USTR Proposes New Section 301 Tariffs on 14 Economies, but Nothing Takes Effect Before January 25
summary: USTR proposed Section 301 tariffs of up to 35% on 14 economies. Nothing takes effect before January 25 hearings. See rates, carveouts, and next steps.
body_markdown:
---


Article


On November 25, 2026, the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) announced that 16 economies run industrial policies that create structural excess capacity in manufacturing, and it proposed new Section 301 tariffs on 14 of them. The announcement is a notice of intent to levy tariffs, not an announcement of tariffs going into effect. USTR will take public comments through January 5, 2027 and hold hearings starting January 25, so no new tariffs take effect before then. Here's what USTR proposed, what the proposal leaves out, and what importers can do while the comment period runs.


## What USTR found


USTR opened these investigations on March 11, 2026 covering 16 economies. After reviewing roughly 1,070 public comments and hearing from nearly 140 witnesses, it determined that practices in 14 of those economies burden U.S. commerce and qualify for action under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. Mexico and Norway were part of the original investigations and don't appear in this round. USTR hasn't said what comes next for either one.


The findings for each country run more than 100 pages with the unique conditions in each country, but two themes show up in every case. Governments in these economies use industrial planning policies to build up manufacturing capacity, and they give their own producers financial advantages over U.S. producers through tax rules, loan rules, grants, currency practices, or forced savings.


## The proposed rates


USTR proposed rates of up to the amounts below. Each one is net of existing capped rates, such as the 15% caps in the trade deals with the EU, Japan, and South Korea, and net of the existing Section 301 forced labor tariff of 10% or 12.5%. In practice, the rate listed is the total for that layer, and the new tariff only adds the difference.

Proposed rate

Up to 18%

Up to 18%

15% cap stays in place

Up to 18%

15% cap stays in place

Up to 18%

15% cap stays in place

15% cap stays in place

Up to 18%

Up to 35%, or 20% if a trade deal is completed


## What the proposal leaves out


The proposal carries the usual carveouts. Goods that already face Section 232 tariffs are excluded, and so are products on the Annex II list, which covers items the U.S. can't source domestically in meaningful quantities. China looks like the exception on Section 232, where the announcement makes no mention of Section 232 tariffs, so it’s unclear whether these tariffs will stack.


China also has a separate list of reductions tied to the[Board of Trade deal](https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/09/u-s-china-board-of-trade/) from earlier this year.


## What happens next


- **January 5, 2027:** Written comments are due, and so are requests to appear at the hearings along with a summary of testimony.
- **January 25, 2027:** USTR holds public hearings on the proposed actions, continuing as needed.
- **After January 25:** USTR can finalize the tariffs. It hasn't announced an effective date, and the final rates could differ from the proposal.


## What importers can do now


Nothing about your duty bill changes today. The comment period still gives you time to prepare, and a few steps make sense now. Start by checking which of your products come from the 14 economies on the list, and pull the Harmonized Tariff Schedule codes for them. Then compare the proposed rates against what you already pay, since the net structure means the added cost varies a lot by country and by product. If one of your suppliers sits in India, Singapore, or Vietnam, keep an eye on trade deal negotiations, because a finished deal lowers the proposed rate. Companies that expect real impact can also file comments or ask to testify before January 5.
